utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Regrettably the last session in this courtroom had to run overtime, so we have a late start. If I could remind you, Mr. Limaj, of the affirmation that you made at the beginning which still applies. Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Whiting:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, at the end of yesterday we looked at Mr. Krasniqi's statements on the 11th and 12th of July in an interview in Koha Ditore and he said in that interview that "the KLA is a regular army, that it has its own staff and its military hierarchy, that it is an organised army." And when those statements were put to you, your answer was that that was not true at the time. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Limaj, do you recall participating in a making of a documentary about is a Sadik Shala?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sadik Shala was killed in Rahovec; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know what date he was killed?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 19th of July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The documentary about Sadik Shala was made and was broadcast in 2002; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It must be like that, because I don't know exactly which year it was. It could be that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have no reason to think it was any other year?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that was after the war?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yes, it was after the war, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were truthful in that documentary?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a description, a general description. You know, like in documentaries you try to give a general description of the personality and the figure of a martyr.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question, Mr. Limaj, was were you truthful in what you said?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And my answer what -- what I just gave, that in these cases when you try to describe the biography of a martyr you try to make a description of his personality. And I tried to say the truth in what I said there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's look at what you said in that documentary about the organisation of the KLA, that the organisation that had been achieved and became public by June 14th, 1998, the date that Jakup Krasniqi made his first public statement. And this is a clip that -- it's from P34. It's clip number 5. I think we need to switch to the Sanction.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "In 1998, Mr. Jakup Krasniqi made his first public appearance as KLA spokesman, which also caused great reverberations in international opinion. "Fatmir Limaj: It is true, the Berisha Mountains have seen special days which were historic dates for the history of the KLA through a spokesman or appearance of a spokesman of the KLA for the first time, Mr. Krasniqi, who from there, from the Shala family, from their Kullas, made his first public announcement in the name of the KLA and as spokesman for the Kosovo Liberation Army. "And I think this was one of the most important moments in our war for liberation because this was the moment when our war for liberation entered a new phase, a phase which would show the world and public opinion at home and abroad that the Kosovo Liberation Army was an organised structure with an authentic political and military structure, with a clear vision and a clear political and military platform, and with people who are capable and ready to go all the way to realise these objectives our success. The importance of the first appearance of Mr. Krasniqi or his first address --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I would like to thank the interpreter for her steadfast effort at trying to keep up with the speed of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't know if it's better with those clips for the interpreter -- if it's better to read it or not. I'm not sure. It does go very quickly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But, Mr. Limaj, there in that documentary you stated that at the occasion when Jakup Krasniqi made his first statement on June 14, 1998, when you were present, you identified that as one of the most important moments in our war for liberation because you could then "show the world abroad and at home that the KLA was an organised structure with an authentic political and military structure." That was true, wasn't it, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is your interpretation, how you interpret the interview. The interview says something else. You -- the things that you mentioned, that it was an important moment and that the KLA was entering a new phase, these are all true. That was a new important phase because the KLA was entering a new part of its life, and after that the events followed. When I spoke about that, I said that it's an important phase for the KLA because the spokesperson spoke for the first time. And secondly, it was important because the KLA was entering this phase when it would become an organised structure and wage a war as an army, and this is how I meant the things I said in the interview.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I can provide the text if you like or we can watch it again, but what you say is that it's a -- and what I submit here is that it's a -- it's a new phase of publicity, that it's the first time, the first public announcement in the name of the KLA and that what this new phase is is making public the KLA and showing the world that the Kosovo Liberation Army was organised and that it had a structure already by the 14th of June, 1998. Isn't that what you're saying there, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, of course the things that I said about Mr. Krasniqi are true. But I also mentioned that the KLA is entering a new phase, and a new phase does not mean just a spokesman coming public. A new phase means organisation entering a new phase of war. And the appearance of Jakup Krasniqi is a symbol of the new event, the new developments in the future. This is how I interpret those words and you can give those words to me again but this is how I interpret them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, the interpretation you put on these words today, there is no obvious relationship between Jakup Krasniqi making a public statement and what you're describing as a coincidental new phase in the war, when in fact in the statement you put the two things together. Jakup Krasniqi is going public with the KLA and what is being revealed to the world is an organised KLA. Isn't that what you were saying, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Please. Please, Your Honours. If you follow the logic of the people who made the documentary, then you will see that they put the Jakup Krasniqi declaration first and then mine. My statement was that the appearance of Jakup Krasniqi in the eyes of the public meant a new phase for the KLA, and that is clear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stay for a moment on the subject of the organisation of the KLA. Do you recall that on the 23rd of February, 1998, Robert Gelbard, Special Envoy from the United States to the region, described the KLA as terrorists? Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, and I also remember another statement that showed that he made a hasty description, because it was a shock to us in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me focus on this first statement, the 23rd of February, for a moment. The KLA reacted to that statement by trying to demonstrate to the world that it was not in fact a terrorist organisation and it was nothing like other so-called terrorist organisations like the IRA or ETA; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA wanted to show something else. The KLA wanted to show that it's an organisation that has one purpose, the liberation of the country. With his actions, it wanted to show that the target of its action were -- was not the territory outside Kosova, it was only the Serbian police and the Serbian army within the territory of Kosova. And personally, I did not like it when KLA was described as a terrorist organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you didn't think that the KLA was a terrorist organisation, did you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did not think that it was a terrorist -- sorry, a terrorist organisation. First it was a guerrilla movement and then it became a spontaneous popular uprising. And then there were steady efforts to make this movement, a movement that would protect the independence of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And just sticking for a moment on the issue of a terrorist organisation, in that respect you don't think the KLA was like the IRA or ETA; correct? It was different from those groups.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I don't know how IRA or ETA are organised, so I can't speak here or analyse what ETA or IRA are. I can't make any distinction or how they are different from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you thought that the IRA and ETA were terrorist organisations and the KLA was not a terrorist organisation; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not what we thought. It was things that were known in the world. People spoke about that. That's what the western world characterised them by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm sorry to interrupt, but I'm interested in what you thought. Is that what you also thought?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying it again. There was nothing to think about, because it was characterised like that by the public opinion in the world, so that's what we were given by the world public opinion, and we did not want to be characterised like them, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You agreed you thought that the KLA was not a terrorist organisation and the IRA or ETA were terrorist organisations, right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am sure that if the KLA went on doing the things that it was doing until then, and if the March event -- events had not happened there would be great danger, great risk that the KLA would be characterised as a terrorist organisation. And the warning of Mr. Gelbard that if the KLA continued on that road it would make the list of terrorists organisation. So the events of March and the mistakes that the Serb authorities and the police made it possible for the KLA not to be described as such, I mean as terrorists. And the KLA did not have at that time clear objectives and clear actions. Well, the KLA was more of a popular uprising. It became a popular uprising, and that is what made us not be described by other people as a terrorist organisation. That's how we escaped that. Although there were an attempt to describe us as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, just to be clear on this point I'm going to show a clip from the interview that we saw yesterday. It's clip number 9 it's on page of P36.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters opted not to translate because of the remarks that were made earlier. So we need to know whether we need to read those passages or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's -- in my opinion, it's better to have them not read. It's easier to have them not read. However, it does create the problem that the transcript that is played is not in the transcript. That, however, can be dealt with later. We can provide the transcript that has been played. But I'm -- I don't know what others think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It seems more practical for it to be provided later and incorporated into the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which will make life a lot easier for the interpreters as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: A very important thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt. On previous occasions where we've played certain clips there has been a recognition between discrepancies between the actual words spoken by the individuals in the clip and the words on the bottom of the clip. So the written words sometimes deviate from what the interpreters have said. So I point that out because it may be of some importance at some point. I'm not wishing to make the interpreters' job any more difficult whatsoever, but I know it's come up in earlier times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We would propose as before to leave it to counsel to identify any such discrepancies if they appear and to discuss it between themselves with a view to resolving it. Most of them, to the extent that they occur, seem not material to the issues in the case. But if there should appear some material difficulty, it might be raised if it can't be resolved between counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you say -- you heard and saw in that clip that you said that the Kosovo Liberation Army had nothing in common with ETA or the IRA or other terrorists organisations; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that the summer developments showed that it became a popular uprising. Well, as far as I know, the developments in Kosova, the summer developments, showed that it had become a popular uprising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Didn't it become a popular uprising after the events in Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was the turning point. It was an important, a key point that triggered the events of summer -- of that summer, summer 1998. I think of course Prekaz is the turning point of later developments, that led to later developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, are you trying to push all of the events further and further into -- later into 1998? That is, events that occurred in March and April you're pushing to the summer and the summer events to the fall? Is that what you're trying to do in your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. In fact, I am willing here, I'm ready to treat the events week by week until summer, even autumn. I can tell you week by week what happened. I'm speaking here about the developments in a period, in a phase. But if you want me to speak about the events week by week, I can do that. But what you're saying, that the KLA was organised earlier, that's not true, because I followed the development of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, let's keep our focus on this clip that we just saw where you talked about the KLA. You said that you were -- you were motivated to show the world that the KLA was not like some other organisations in Europe and had nothing in common with ETA and the IRA. And that was at the time, that is in February and March, you were trying to show the world that you were not like ETA and the IRA; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were trying to show the world that we did not have terrorist objectives. Even earlier, not only in March and April, as you're saying. No organisation would like to be called terrorist, but the statement Mr. Gelbard made rang an alarm bell. It was very dangerous for us because it came from a well-known personality. So there was continuous danger at that time that the KLA would be described as terrorist, although we did not want it to be like that. But as I said, later developments made us become otherwise. So we were not described as terrorists because of later developments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, on the second day of your testimony you described the KLA in the early months, let's say March, April, May, as being a guerrilla army.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified on the third day of your testimony, when you were talking about Rahovec, you said that the KLA was still a guerrilla army. You said Rahovec shows that the KLA was still a long way from being -- from being responsive to the new reality. It had remained still under total confusion, a guerrilla unit. Do you remember that testimony, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said it a little differently. I said that Rahovec is an example that shows the confusion that reigned supreme at that time. But events of -- after the 29th of May -- the KLA, after the 29th of May did not have either guerrilla units or any kind of units, and you here are trying to say that the KLA was well organised and so on. So it was the events of that time that rang the alarm bell and told us that we had to get organised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the 29th of May, the KLA started fighting a frontal war, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean by frontal war. I said that on the 29th of May without any military operation, Malisheva -- Malisheva [as interpreted] prevented the Serbian forces from entering Malisheva because different units were placed at the entrance of Malisheva.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. What I mean by a frontal war is KLA engaging the Serb forces directly, in a frontal fashion. That was the strategy after the 29th May, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the units were placed at this point, there have been Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. confrontations in several cases. But in some other cases there were no confrontations until the end of July. For example, in Rahovec, there were no confrontations at all until the Rahovec fighting. The same with Klina. There have been confrontations in Blace from the direction of Duhla, and there have been confrontations in the Lapusnik gorge time and again and also in several points.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And those were frontal confrontations, not guerrilla confrontations; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when these points were established there, that was frontal confrontation, because it was known that the KLA was placed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ramiz Qeriqi testified that on the 14th of June - which, incidentally, is the same date that you were talking about in the clip that we saw earlier today when you were talking about Jakup Krasniqi's first public declaration - "On the 14th of June," he said, "we came out openly as an army. It was a frontal war." He said -- in this courtroom he said, "From the 14th of June when we went on a frontal attack it was no longer guerrilla warfare." You agree with that, right, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, this is an example of how things developed. From Likovc to Malisheva, these were how things developed. This is an example until the date that Mr. Prosecutor is speaking about here. Until that date this was a guerrilla unit. But after that, it became out [as interpreted] and carried out public actions if I can call them and created a line. And in fact, if I may say so, they copied or they did what other units did in other places. But in the beginning, they were a guerrilla unit and did the same things that the other guerrilla units did in other places.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So guerrilla -- guerrilla warfare; but that changed in the middle of June 1998. That's your testimony.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. That is the phase we're entering -- we were entering. The KLA, from guerrilla activities, was entering a new phase, new circumstances, and the General Staff was not ready to respond to this uprising, to what was happening on the terrain. So in the beginning they functioned as guerrilla units, but after that they entered a new phase and there were attempts made to find other ways of organising the KLA. And even the meeting with Mr. Krasniqi was about this. The events on the terrain showed that --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you. I think you've answered the question. Let's go back to the subject of collaborators. You agree, don't you, with what Mr. Jakup Krasniqi said in this courtroom that commanders in the KLA had the discretion to identify and deal with collaborators? And I'll read you more specifically what he said. He said, "The operational units were separated from each other. But they could make their own decisions. When a person was harmful to the KLA, when such a person is giving information on the movements of the KLA to the Belgrade regime, in these instances the unit had all the power of discretion to conduct such acts without any -- without taking the extra approval or supplementary approval for such acts." That's how it was, wasn't it, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can interpret Mr. Krasniqi's statement as you wish, but what I'm saying here what I know and what I've been through. Your Honours, as for attacks against the Serb police, this was direct attacks because we were in war with the Serb police and those who participated actively with the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about collaborators.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're -- Mr. Prosecutor, you have mystified the term "collaborator" so much here, and to tell you the truth, I don't even know whether my parent here is considered as a collaborator here as well. I am speaking of those collaborators who participated actively in violence, in raids, in murders together with the Serbian police. And those were an objective, a target for us. And these are the collaborators for me, but others, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm not talking about who are collaborators, I'm just talking about who had the power to decide who were collaborators. And what I'm putting to you, Mr. Limaj -- Mr. Limaj, please listen to my question. I'm putting to what Mr. Krasniqi said and that is that individual commanders had the power to decide who was and who was not a collaborator. You agree with that, don't you, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am given trying to explain this to you. For us, collaborators were those who were active with the Serbian police. We were in open war with them. There wasn't any special request from the staff for someone to fight the Serbian police, and whoever was fighting with the police, together with the police, they were our target, our military target. This is what I understand. And what Mr. Krasniqi understood, then that I don't know. And if you're trying to interpret this differently, then I do not agree with you because my entire activity shows the different side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, you're still not listening to my question. My question is: Who had the power to decide who was a collaborator? It was individual commanders. They could decide if somebody in their village or in their area was a collaborator; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will try to give you my answer again. In a certain village, let's say, in case the Serbian police and collaborators attacked the population or undertook an operation the commander of that unit was permitted to take actions against that police unit or to attack police patrols or launch a direct attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And, Mr. Limaj, you agree with Mr. Krasniqi, don't you, that there were no procedures, no -- there was no trial, there was no investigation, there was no hearing afforded to people who were accused of collaboration, was there?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree fully that at that time we lacked these things, but I don't know what you mean by people who were accused. As for those who participated directly, there's no need for that; but as for others, then I agree fully that there weren't any such proceedings and trials at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's talk about -- let's go back and talk about when you came to Kosovo. Before you came to Kosovo in March of 1998, you were living with Ismet Jashari in Switzerland; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not living with Ismet Jashari in Switzerland. I lived alone, but I was in contact with him. We knew each other. I went to visit him. He came to visit me. We went together on gatherings. So we socialised. We met there. I did not live in Ismet Jashari's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever live with him for any period of time either in his house or some other place in Switzerland?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be, Your Honours, until I found an apartment because we were changing apartments. Maybe I might make a mistake here, but it is possible when we were moving from one apartment in one city to another to -- it was possible for me to stay for a week with a friend or with family, and this could have happened for four or five days or maximum one week until I found my own apartment. However, I later on had my own apartment. And I had my nephews and most of the time I stayed with my nephews. I stayed mostly at Haxhi Shala's place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your nephews, which nephews are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to my nephews that we mentioned two, three days ago, my nephews from Klecka. Because part of them lived in Switzerland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me their names?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- correction I lived at Shefqet's place, Shefqet Shala's place. Shefqet lived in Lausanne, and since I was there as well I lived with him. And then Dalip, Skender, these are the nephews with whom I stayed, whom I visited. But those of the time I lived with Shefqet because he was in Lausanne. And as I was living there, too --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's Shefqet Shala, Dalip Shala and Skender Shala?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are brothers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified you decided to come back to Kosovo after the events at the end of February, beginning of March; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is that the events in March accelerated this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You already had plans to come back to Kosovo, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I had such a plan. I wanted -- whenever I was given the opportunity to return back to Kosova I was thinking of going back to Kosova, but as circumstances were such it wasn't -- impossible for me to go there immediately. I had to find the appropriate moment to go back and that was when the Prekaz events took place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that when you decided to go back you contacted Adem Grabovci; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We used to see each other quite frequently with Adem Grabovci on these gatherings for fund-raising, but we also spent some time together at Bardhyl Mahmuti's place. I know that Adem Grabovci travelled frequently to Albania. He had such connections. And he was trying to offer me the opportunity and to find me the proper route to go back to Kosovo through Albania.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, if you focus on just answering my question this will be a lot faster. Otherwise it's going to take a very, very long time, okay? After you decided to go, you contacted Adem Grabovci; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long after you contacted him did you actually go to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, I think it was the gathering in Geneva after the protests in Geneva in front of the UN building in Geneva. I think it was that day. Many Albanians had gathered in front of the UN building to show their revolt for the events in Kosova. I'm not sure now about the date, but it was 5 or 6th, around this date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What, on the 5th or 6th of March that's when you told -- that's when you spoke with Adem Grabovci?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should be around this date, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you left around the 11th of March; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken because you should bear in mind I may give you the wrong date. I tried to go back once, but I missed the flight, and the following day I took another flight. It should be around this date, the 10th or 11th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that you told your nephews in Switzerland that you were going to London.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And are these the nephews that we were talking about just a moment ago, these same nephews?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm going to show another clip from P34, the documentary on Sadik Shala. This is from page 1.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, Mr. Limaj, in fact you were planning from November 1997 to go back to Kosovo; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. The truth is different, and I will explain it here before you. As I said, my idea was to go back to Kosovo and Prekaz accelerated my attempts. But what you're trying to put to me here from this documentary, the idea was whenever we would go back we didn't want that person to be surprised. In fact, Rexhep Selimi could go to this place as well because he knew that they were my nephews. And the same with me. The idea was not for them to be surprised. Whoever goes to them, we didn't want them to be surprised.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's also -- it's not true, is it, that you told your nephews that you were going to London. You told Skender in November that you would be coming to Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is Skender saying here that I was going to Klecke, and is he saying that I'm going to Klecka as a KLA member? Skender is saying something totally different. He's saying that Fatmir told me there is a possibility for three up known persons to come there and to Skender I was not an unknown person. I was his uncle. And here he is not saying that three persons are going or who is going there. And from that perspective, Skender is then saying that later on Daja, Haxhi and Kumanova came. Please make -- separate the moments. This is produced in 2002 and reproduces some events that took part in the past. I did not tell my nephews. I told them that I was going to London in order to raise funds for Vendlindja Therret, Homeland is Calling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What Skender actually says in the tape is that you told him you were -- that three people would come in November and that two or three months later it happened and you and Haxhi Shala and Ismet Jashari came. So at least he thought you were talking about yourself. That's what he thought, that you were saying that you were coming.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm saying here that I was a witness to that event. The reality is not what is seen on this video. I'm telling you for a fact that his family, they didn't know that he was in Kosovo until June and let alone this. We did say three persons and he's saying secret, unknown. This is true that it happened, but it's not that he didn't know who was going or when that person was going. And please separate the moments.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no need to confuse things here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that clip you also talk about the importance of the area of Klecka and Divjak to the General Staff; right? You're nodding your head yes.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in fact, the General Staff moved around during the months of May, June, and July, but one of the places it operated from was from Divjak, correct? During those months.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can say that from the day when Mr. Krasniqi was proclaimed a spokesperson this place can be considered as one of the bases of the KLA, which was first a temporary basis [as interpreted] and later on it was a permanent one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Rexhep Selimi was on the General Staff at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said this yesterday as well. As representatives of the General Staff, we had no idea what a general staff meant. I had no idea what a general staff meant regardless of our background.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As a representative --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question was simple. He was a member of the General Staff in May 1998; correct? You know that now.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is simple as well. I knew that Rexhep Selimi was a member of a general staff, a full member in November 1998 when I was told about my membership as well. Before that date, I didn't know that he was a full member of the General Staff. I only knew that he was a representative of the General Staff, and this is the logic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in November 1998, you learned that he had -- that in fact he had been a full member of the General Staff for some time; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. He was a member of the General Staff, but we didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He stated in an interview that the General Staff operated -- one of the places it operated from was from Divjak starting in May of 1998. Again I'm going to suggest to you, Mr. Limaj, that you're pushing the dates further and further into 1998 at every opportunity. In fact, it was in May of 1998 when the General Staff started operating in Klecke; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. You're trying to represent me as such here. I'm -- in my statement, I said that the KLA, the General Staff had a base, a KLA base -- not in May 1998 but in May 1997, and I also mentioned the name of the owner of that house, Mr. Zogaj who was arrested around the same time when my brother Demir was arrested. So as a base it existed even before in Divjak, near Klecke. But I didn't know that. And in that house it's there where the General Staff settled, and that house today is a museum. It's not true that I'm pushing you further and further into 1998, but I'm taking you back to 1997 and telling you that that base had KLA representatives even at that time. I'm just telling you the way how things developed. It is possible that Rexhep Selimi was in Divjak, because this came to be true later on. It is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I'll read to you what Rexhep Selimi said. He said that from March until May, the general headquarters was in the region of Drenica in the zone that they were discussing, but from this day, from May, it passed in the zone of Pashtrik to the Berisha Mountains in the village of Divjak. In May -- in May of 1998, the General Staff started -- one of the places it started operating from was Divjak; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I'm speaking for myself here, until the public appearance of Jakup Krasniqi, I did not know that representatives or members of the General Staff had a base in Divjak. As I said, the representatives of the General Staff came to my base. Until that time, I didn't know that they had a base in Divjak, and I found out about that after Mr. Jakup Krasniqi settled there in that base and after it became a seat for the KLA General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back, Mr. Limaj, to your trip to Kosovo in March of 1998, you testified that you travelled to Albania with Haxhi Shala and Ismet Jashari, but -- but that you had no plans to continue with them to Kosovo. That was your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you arrived in Albania, you met up with a large group and you went into Kosovo with this large group of approximately 30 people; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there were some very impressive people in that group; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some that I knew, yes, and who later I learned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hashim Thaqi and Kadri Veseli the two men who you say led the group were in fact at that time on the General Staff of the KLA; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time we didn't know that they were members of the General Staff. And this should be clear to you. Make separations. Separate the time. Don't confuse me. I'm telling you clearly. At that time we didn't know that they were members of the General Staff. I didn't even know what was Hashim Thaqi's name, and I didn't even know what was Kadri Veseli's name. I didn't know their names. I had seen them in Switzerland during a gathering, but I didn't know his name.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You learned later that they were members of the General Staff at that time; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September 1998, I think it was around this time, Your Honours, the General Staff came out with a statement in which Mr. Hashim Thaqi was appointed political representative of the General Staff, and it's then when I learned that he was a member of the General Staff. And later on I learned that he was the leader of the political wing of the directorate, correction, of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's just talk about today. You knew that when you travelled with Hashim Thaqi and Kadri Veseli in March of 1998, they were members of the General Staff at that time. You know that now; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Adem Grabovci, he later became a member of the General Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Adem Grabovci and myself became members of the General Staff on the same date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Fehmi Lladrovci, Shukri Buja, Haxhi Shala, Ismet Jashari all became important commanders within the KLA; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This shows you the situation in which the KLA was, the level at which it was before we went and when we went, because there was no other who could deal with the organisation at that time to bring the KLA activities into life. And it is true that the majority were appointed later on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, the truth is that this group didn't just happen to come together but this group was brought together, wasn't it? This group was organised.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think it was a coincidence, not in the way you're thinking. They were people who were ready to self-sacrifice. It was not that they were organised or that someone ordered them to go there. It was because they were willing and ready to sacrifice themselves because the Jashari family had given them the example of sacrifice, and we were thinking that by sacrificing ourselves the issue of Kosova would be internationalised. And this is how I thought, Your Honours. I was ready to sacrifice myself for my country and hoping that my sacrifice would open the eyes of the public.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, I'm not talking about the motivation of the people in the group. I'm talking about the fact that this group was brought together. These people didn't just happen to arrive in Albania all at the same time ready to go to Kosovo. This group was organised and brought together; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by coincidence?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I mean is that the -- these people were told to come at a certain time. They were told that there would be a group coming at a certain time and they came from Switzerland and elsewhere to travel to Albania at the same time.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. After the March events, after the killing of Adem Jashari, hundreds of thousands of people wanted to join the KLA. Hundreds of thousands of people from the streets wanted to join. That's why it's not true what you're saying. We did meet in Tirana. Someone had organised that trip. Someone had organised the passing of the -- the crossing of the border. There's no dilemma about that. But it's not true what you're saying that someone was designated to organise these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the trip was not just organised from Albania. It was organised from Switzerland; correct? That is, these people arrived in Albania at the same time because they were organised to arrive in Albania at the same time and travel to Kosovo. They had been selected to travel to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, they were not selected. I'm telling you the truth. I don't want to speculate about others, but I'm telling you my story. Who selected Haxhi Shala and Ismet Jashari? I went. They came with me to Albania. It's when they came to Albania it's then that they realised that I was going to Kosovo and that I was a member of the KLA, and it's then when they heard it for the first time from my mouth. And I cannot speak on others' behalf because then that would be speculation. As to how others were organised, I don't know but I'm speaking of my own experience. But as you're saying it was then when lists were made, when uniforms were started to be purchased. But at the time when we went, Your Honours, except for myself and these two guys, they only knew and found out about that in Albania where I was going. I don't want to speculate about Fehmi or other friends, but I know the truth about myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, because we had a late start I assume we have a late break or would you prefer to remain with the schedule or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will break at about 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that when you entered Kosovo you and your group went to Drenica because, as you said, that's where the fighting was going on. Do you remember testifying to that? You said that the only address was Drenica.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly. The only address to which we could go was Drenica, and we headed to Drenica because the fighting was going on in Drenica. Drenica was known as a place that had KLA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You arrived with a weapon and a bag of ammunition; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a bag of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And specifically you went to Likovc.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, these two or three villages, there are two or three villages in a row. I didn't know at the time where I was, but later on I learned that it was Likovc. We arrived at 3.00 or 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you arrived in Likovc, you said -- you testified that you found the people there scared because they feared retaliation from the Serbs. Do you remember that testimony on your first day in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor, because at the time Serbia had only already surrounded part of Drenica. Events had taken place. Not only Likoshan and Qirez had seen massacres and that's why this was evident with the population, with the local population of these villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that they were not capable of protecting their village. Do you remember that, remember testifying to that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You testified that the situation was very grave.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony, then, is that seeing this, arriving at this situation with a weapon and ammunition, seeing a scared population that could not protect itself, you then had the idea on your own to head in the opposite direction and go to your village of Klecke which you described in your testimony as a "remote, mountainous village." Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Let us be clear. After we arrived at Likovc, as you described it, that was the situation there. Your Honours, civilian population were standing guard duty in the village. And this was even happening in the 1990s in Kosova. But as people who had come from the west, we wanted to meet KLA representatives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's keep our focus on March of 1998, okay? If -- your testimony is that seeing this grave situation, population that feared retaliation, that could not protect itself, you went -- instead you decided on your own to go to a remote mountainous village, in the opposite direction. Is that your testimony, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, I'm not saying this, and you're trying to impose that on me. Your Honours, the situation was such -- fear was evident. There's no dilemma about that. We stayed there for a week. It was a poor village. Villages did not have the means to support themselves let alone us. Seeing this reality and seeing that a part of Serbian forces was withdrawing, we decided to leave Likovc. This is the truth. And we wanted to begin with our military activities so that to avoid the possibility of the Serb forces to localise the attacks only in one area. This was our reason -- these were our reasons for leaving Likovc. It was not that people were frightened and that's why we left. We went there in order to sacrifice ourselves for them, for that -- for the people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The truth, Mr. Limaj, is that you were sent from Likovc to accomplish a bigger mission, isn't it, for the KLA, that is to organise the area in the other parts of Drenica.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you already, Mr. Prosecutor, because the situation was such I decided to go to a place where I could operate, to my own municipality. It was in our interest to expand the war, to expand the ranks of the KLA. Simply, Malisheve was my municipality. I was going back to my birthplace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were sent by the KLA to that area. You were sent there.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You should know how guerrilla warfare operates and what a guerrilla units means. By the nature, the very nature of the guerrilla warfare, it is logical for a small group - two, three like we were - to go there to find a base where they could shelter, to carry out the action and come back to the base. Secondly, the task is to recruit another person in order to expand. And these are the activities that we performed at that time. I didn't know at that time of any person who was member of the KLA in that region.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sylejman Selimi stated in his interview he said -- referring to you he said, "Naturally I think he," Fatmir Limaj, "had some sort of directive in the General Staff to create the units." That's true, isn't it? You had a directive.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not saying here anything differently. What I'm saying is that we met with Mr. Rexhep Selimi. I said to him, "Rexhep, there's no need for me to stay here. I will contribute more to the KLA if I start with the activities in my area." And he agreed with my idea. And from this conversation, I set off for my municipality. Of course I didn't leave Likovc without telling where I was going. We discussed the best interests for us. I wanted to find out about their experience, to exchange experiences.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It wasn't just Rexhep Selimi. It was Rexhep Selimi and Hashim Thaqi; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. I think that Hashim was present during the second meeting if I'm in the mistaken. Maybe he was present in both meetings but I don't remember. I know that he was present in one of them. I knew that he was there with Shukri, because he addressed me with Shukri. He told me to take him up to a part where he could pass to his own municipality. Hashim was there as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, since you raise Shukri, Shukri Buja stated that you were appointed to lead a group to Klecke and the purpose of the group was to organise the KLA in the area of Suva Reka and Malisheva, but you were appointed to do that job by Rexhep Selimi and Hashim Thaqi. That's what Shukri Buja says. It's in evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm telling you the truth. Your Honours, I couldn't have led the group from Drenica to Malisheve, neither could Shukri Buja because he doesn't know the terrain and not even Ismet Jashari because it was the first time he was in that terrain. Not even Haxhi Shala because he was for years in Switzerland. So even myself I didn't know that road, but at least I had a better knowledge than the others. But if you want, I have been the leader of this group up to Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just interpose before we rise, just one matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: I've listened very carefully to the cross-examination so far yesterday and today, and the method of cross-examination here I would submit is misleading, and many in jurisdictions the idea that you put to a witness what another witness says for comment is usually prohibited. However, I understand here there's a different approach. If, in fact, what is going to happen, and it happened yesterday, a selection of witnesses so far are put before this witness - this is a very good example - in order to make a point, which is more of a speech point than anything else, then I would ask that Mr. Whiting puts all the other witnesses that deal with this very point, one of which he's just mentioned, who was disclosed very late, and that is what Mr. Thaqi says about this very point. At the end of the day, there isn't a clear position, and that -- Mr. Whiting was present at that particular interview, then these matters must be put fairly and squarely, in my submission. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. We will adjourn and resume at twenty past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Before you commence, Mr. Whiting, could I indicate, Mr. Mansfield, we feel there is no reason to take any action in respect of your words before we broke. It is a matter which can be dealt with clearly in final address and even, if necessary, at some particular matters in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MANSFIELD
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, focusing constituent on when you arrive in Likovc. You testified on the second day in this courtroom that when you arrived in Likovc "You were eager to hear from Rexhep," meaning Rexhep Selimi, as to "what to do, how to act when we arrived there." Remember that testimony on the second day?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, yes. I said here today that we discussed and we wanted to know what the situation was. We wanted to know what the reality was and how things were going. We discussed as friends and with others too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were eager to hear from Rexhep because you knew already then that he was a higher person in the KLA; right, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, sir. I wanted to talk to Rexhep because he was a schoolmate. He was a friend of -- of the schooltime, and it was quite normal to talk to him. And I thought that he -- he was going to tell me how things were going, as a friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You wanted to know from him "what to do, how to act." That's -- those are your words. You wanted to find out from him "what to do." Isn't that right, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After those days we sat to talk about the situation. Why should I stay here? It would be better for me to go to my municipality. What do you think about this move? And he agreed with my idea that it would be better to go to my municipality in Malisheve.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, Shukri Buja stated and it's in evidence, it's P160, page 24, he said that at this time when you were in Likovc he said, "Fatmir Limaj was assigned the task of coordinating work with the General Staff while I had to coordinate with Fatmir." That's what happened in Likovc; right? You were assigned to coordinate with the General Staff, and the others like Shukri were assigned to coordinate with you; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not true. I heard him say otherwise in spite of what you're saying. What I've heard him say is different, and he cannot lie in front of me, and the truth is the one I'm saying, and it's not true what you're saying. But he has said it differently. It's different from what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He can't lie in front of you or he can't tell the truth in front of you, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about this Court, this Chamber, in front of this Chamber.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about what you said, "in front of me." He can't lie in front of you or he can't tell the truth in front of you, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, in spite of all efforts, all efforts that you have done to terrorise me and my family, you must realise that the strength of the argument is on my side. You are trying to put pressure on me, and this is not true. The truth is the one that I'm saying, Mr. Prosecutor. I'm saying it again. That man has said the truth and the reality in front of this Chamber, and he knew what the truth was, and he knew that my Defence would use arguments to support that. Please do not try to change and misinterpret my words, please.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, Haxhi Shala, Topi, when he was interviewed he said that when he went to Drenica as part of your group he was appointed by the General Staff to supply weapons from Albania to Kosovo, that that would be his job when you all went to Klecke. That's what he said in his interview, and that you were, in April of 1998, you were the commander in Klecka and that you were responsible for the organisation in the Malisevo area. That's what Haxhi Shala said in his interview. That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not truth. Why don't you bring Haxhi Shala to testify here? He will tell you what the truth is. The truth is after April, in June, sometime in June it happened. Your Honours, after that great amount of people started to get organised, then people started to think about it because some people sent money. Some people went to buy weapons in Albania. Then the General Staff issued an order there should be two units who will be responsible for supplying weapons, and this happened sometime in June when the road of Junik was opened. It's not possible in April or May.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Limaj, you're pushing forward the dates of all these events. The events that occurred in March you're now saying occurred in June. Isn't that what you're doing here, Mr. Limaj?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. I'm trying to tell you what the situation was. You are trying to change the direction of things. The truth is this: In March, what can I say -- what -- what weapons do we need for three people in March? Up until after the 9th of May, we were about seven people, and we were in deep secrecy. We operated in deep secrecy. The activity that was taking place at the time I told you, things happened later, and this is the reality. It is common knowledge in Kosova. When roads started to be opened and -- Junik is on the border with Albania, and at that time people started to move stuff with lorries and mules and everything. It was the end of June and the beginning of July. That's when the offensive started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's stay focused on April if we could, Mr. Limaj. In -- after you went to Klecka and, I submit, to coordinate matters with the General Staff, you remained in contact with Rexhep Selimi in Likovc in April; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, your suggestions are incorrect, and I cannot accept them. Whereas my movements, Your Honours, of course after I went to Klecka in March, time after time I went to Drenica, contacted with Rexhep, sometimes with Sylejman, sometimes with Muje Krasniqi, Muse Jashari, depending on who was around. It's true. But it's not as you say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April you went several times to Likovc; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we were on two or three in Likovc, in Likovc. For the first time it was the end of April. It was Rexhep Selimi, because he had to go somewhere. I can't remember where, but he was in transit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You think the first time you went back to Likovc was at the end of April?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Rexhep Selimi came to Likovc in April for the first time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm talking about your trips to Likovc. You went to Likovc several times in April; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you. Two or three times during April. It may be one more time, but two, three, at the most four, because it was difficult, Your Honours. We operated in deep secrecy. To go from Klecke to Likovc -- Jusuf Jashari was injured because it was a difficult trip. It had to be done at night, and we were very limited and restrained in our movements at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you told us that Rexhep Selimi came to Klecke for the first time at the end of April.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately. Yes, it should be for the first time. After the 20th of April, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you said a moment ago that you were operating in deep secrecy; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you testified before that secrecy was one of the reasons that you and other members of the KLA wore masks.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You -- in your case you continued to wear masks until the 9th of May; right?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know -- you know that others in the KLA wore masks even after that date; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here it depends of when we are talking about. We should clarify the circumstances. For example, after the 9th of May, for the first time we -- we came out during the day without masks. We -- we used the masks, but it was then that we removed them. I'm talking about ourselves. Whereas in Malisheva there were still units who were in secrecy, operating in secrecy, because the points were not set up in Malisheva. Where there were Serb checkpoints around, then the masks were needed. And we're talking about the 15th of June in Kroimire, that depended on how the events moved.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in addition to wearing masks, you used pseudonyms to protect your identities?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You would also hide your role or your function from those who did not need to know what your functions were; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What roles are you talking about when we had a unit of three people? Who were we going to hide stuff from? Because we were friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For example, you told us earlier today that Rexhep Selimi was a member of the General Staff but you didn't find that out until November of 1998.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, we should make a distinction here. It's not the same as member of the General staff or member of the guerrilla unit. And Rexhep Selimi as a member of General Staff, he did not reveal his identity because it was a different importance. But a guerrilla unit that we were, we were only three people, and we -- we couldn't hide anything from each other.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, my question was about the KLA in general, about -- it wasn't about you. It was about the KLA in general, that people -- commanders in the KLA would, as part of this deep secrecy, would hide their role -- for example, Rexhep Selimi and others would hide their roles from those who did not need to know what their role was, what their function was. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not accurate. The units are a different thing, and the General Staff is another thing. In the case of the General Staff, yes, but in the case of the units there is nothing to hide. Everybody has -- has shown the fact that they were members of the KLA. And if there are five people in the unit, one is the leader and that's known.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand. I'm talking about people with roles, for example, on the General Staff or other commanding roles. They would hide their functions from those who did not need to know; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There have been no commanding roles or functions. They were members of the guerrilla units, and you know that there were no commanding roles. And the international opinion knows that, but you are trying to introduce something which did not exist. Please, Mr. Prosecutor, let's not say things which did not exist. In spite of the attempts you're making, these are things that did not exist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm just trying to find out the truth, Mr. Limaj. Speaking about the General Staff, they would hide their roles, and they did that -- they hid their roles until November; correct? The members of the General Staff hid their roles until approximately November of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if someone knew who -- who was a member of the General Staff, you had all these educated people like Hashim Thaqi, Krasniqi and others who had university degrees, and we -- we are not talking about a General Staff with military trained people. This is my opinion. As for the units they are quite a different thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You are answering a different question than the one I put to you. My question simply was: The members of the General Staff they hid their roles from those who did not need to know until approximately November of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. For example, we should -- Hashim Thaqi and another group, they came out in September or October as political representatives, whereas other representatives like, for example, the -- Rexhep Selimi as a general inspector of the army, I heard that later on. And that was December, when he became -- when I knew that he was a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So your testimony is that there were many people even within -- who were within the KLA who did not know who was a member of the General Staff; correct? Before November 1998.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now -- now there are people who say there are -- we started the war with Adem Jashari and that's how we fought the war. But I must say that very few are the people who knew who the members of the General Staff were. And then after the war ended, then everybody started talking as if they knew things, who the members were. But at the time, for the time that we are talking about, very few people knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And one reason to maintain this kind of secrecy was so that the Serb forces, the Serb authorities, would not find out who these people were; correct? That was one reason to maintain secrecy.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, one of the reasons. That was one. It was their families who were affected. And if the Yugoslav army knew who were organising the war, and it would be much easier for them to crush the uprising.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course. And that also -- as a result of that secrecy, it was also difficult for others, for outsiders, to know who were the members of the General Staff, who were the commanders of the KLA; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying it again. We -- within the KLA we didn't know, let alone the outsiders.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just to focus back again on the secrecy for the ordinary soldier, let's say, the masks, the pseudonym. That secrecy was also to protect the members of the KLA from Serb forces, from Serb authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this was in territories which were under Serbian control or where there were families exposed to danger.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And would you agree, Mr. Limaj, with what Shukri Buja said in his testimony here in this courtroom? He said that one strategy that was used by the Serb police was to attempt to compromise Albanians by bringing them to the police station repeatedly and then -- forcing them to come to the police station repeatedly and then spreading rumours that they were giving information. That was one tactic that was used by the Serb police. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I cannot speculate. Anything could have happened under the rule of the secret police, Serbian secret police, or under the rule of that regime. They have used different methods that you cannot think of. Anything that one could bring to mind, they have used it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Certainly one method that you would -- one method that you were aware of was what Ramadan Behluli described in this courtroom when he said that the Serbian MUP tried to get information from Albanians about the KLA by interrogating them in the streets or in the police departments. That was certainly one tactic that you were familiar with; correct?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was done as a rule by the Serbian police. They were interested in finding information. And that was especially happening in territories under their control. This happened where they -- in territories where they knew that there was KLA movements, and they -- they have done this to villages in my area too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's go back to March and April and May. Well, let's -- March and April of 1998. In fact, Mr. Limaj, you've described yourself repeatedly as a guerrilla commander of just a few men during that time period, but in fact you were one of the early -- one of the early leaders of the KLA. You're laughing.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm laughing because --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You've considered yourself one of the early leaders of the KLA; correct? You've described yourself that way.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry because I laughed, but I laughed because of this: Your Honours, when we went to Klecka, we were only three people and we did not have a leader. And if we had had a leader, he would have told us, "You have to wake up in the morning, do this during the day," and I wouldn't be able to deal with that. The only motive to go there, to enter the country, was to do something for my country, to come to the aid of my people, and I was ready to sacrifice my own life for that. I was ready to sacrifice myself for the Kosova cause. I had no idea. I had no preparation. All my life speaks about a different orientation. But there was nobody else in the long-run. We saw it later on, there was nobody else. So that's why I had to do the things that I have done.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Limaj, after the events in Prekaz --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't see myself as a leader.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, we'll get back to that in a moment. But after the events in Prekaz, there were many, many men in Kosovo, men and boys in Kosovo who were joining the KLA. Not just you. Not just you and the three men in Klecka but --

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- many, many.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm not saying that there were only three of us all the time. I'm speaking about my experience. At that time, I did not know that there were other people. I am sure about this. You're asking me about myself, and I'm showing you or I'm telling you about my experience. I told me about my thoughts at the time, the situation. Of course the Prekaz events brought many people to our ranks. Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. Many people started joining after the events of Prekaz. Just like you did. There were many other people in Kosovo who started joining the KLA, correct, after Prekaz?

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Prosecutor. But this happened time after time. It didn't happen overnight. You can't just push a button and bring people. For example, after the Prekaz massacre, the protests started. Popular protests in Pristina, and then they expanded to other cities outside Kosova as well, in Albania. Wherever Albanians lived. And he there was the women's protests. So everything increased. The revolt increased. So after the Prekaz events, hundreds of thousands of people came out in Pristina and cheered slogans in favour of the KLA. So this also happened in the west. And if I may continue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, I think you've answered the question. Let's move on to other questions, otherwise we'll be here, as I said, for a very long time. Mr. Limaj, let's go back who how described yourself from a leader from the start. I'm going to show you another clip. It's P36.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So there, Mr. Limaj, you described yourself -- you were asked if you and Hashim Thaqi and the others were in fact the real leadership of the KLA from the very beginning and you said, "Of course, of course."

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. We have to interpret this as it is. It says clearly here "the group," and amongst this group there were people like Hashim, and Kadri Veseli, Fehmi Lladrovci, Sami Lushtaku and others. And as I said, Your Honours, these 30 people --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, sir. Yes, of course, I was there. It's a well known fact that I was there. So when we entered, these were people who were ready to sacrifice, and of course because they were ready to sacrifice, some people of this group became one of the key figures of the KLA. I'm mentioning one thing here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but you say that -- in this clip you say that you were the real leadership of the KLA from the very beginning. Not that you became leaders, but that you were the real leadership from the very beginning. And that's how it was, wasn't it, Mr. Limaj? You and the others you've mentioned, you were the real leadership from the beginning.

utterances.speaker: FATMIR LIMAJ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not true. It's about Hashim here, yes, and that is true, but later on some of us became leaders in the war. Hashim, Kadri, Fehmi Lladrovci, they were. In fact Fehmi Lladrovci was not a commander there or in the General Staff. But Hashim Thaqi and Kadri Veseli were from the beginning til the end. And in fact, Hashim Thaqi came out as the political leader of the KLA. He was also in Rambouillet. But if you're trying to say that all of us were leaders from that moment, in the beginning, no, that's not true, Mr. Prosecutor. This group went into Kosovo. Seventy per cent of the people of this group later became commanders of the zones, of brigades, as well as member of the General Staff, and this is the context of what I was saying there about the leadership of the KLA. And I couldn't just give dates there to say that this person was a member or a leader from this date on or the other person was a member of General Staff or a leader from the beginning or from the middle of the war. These are facts that everybody in Kosova knows.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
